identity.title: The Computer Does Exactly What You Say
identity.description: Give precise instructions in the correct order and predict the resulting outcome.

learning.startingState: Assumes computers understand human intentions and can fill in missing details.
learning.targetState: Understands that computers follow instructions literally in sequential order to produce outcomes.

completionCriteria: Distinguish general goals from precise instructions
Sequence dependent actions in proper order
Identify flawed instructions that produce unintended outcomes
masteryCriteria: Explain why an instruction sequence fails when a prerequisite step is out of order

content.title: Meet the World's Most Literal Assistant
content.hook: You: “Make me a sandwich.” Computer: “Sure.” It puts two slices of bread on the table and stops.
content.context: It didn't fail. You left out the instructions. The computer doesn't know what you meant—it follows the instructions you give it.
goals: See why computers need exact steps, not general goals
Arrange actions in the exact order needed to produce an outcome

content.question:
Look at this sequence:
1. Put bread on the plate.
2. Put cheese on the bread.
3. Put another piece of bread on top.

What will you have?

options.text: A sandwich
A glass of water
A plate with cheese beside the bread
Nothing

content.explanation: Each instruction changes the situation step by step until the final outcome is reached.

feedback.correct: Exactly. Each step changed the situation to produce the final outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Think through the steps in order: bread, then cheese, then top bread.

content.question:
Now look at this sequence:
1. Put cheese on the bread.
2. Put bread on the plate.

What is missing or wrong?

options.text: The first slice of bread was never placed on the plate before the cheese
The cheese is the wrong type
There are too many steps
You need a glass of water first

content.explanation: The computer can only do what the instructions say. If a prerequisite step is missing, the outcome is broken.

feedback.correct: Right. You can't put cheese on bread that isn't there yet.
feedback.incorrect: Look at step 1: where is the bread sitting when the cheese goes on?

content.prompt: Arrange these instructions to pour a glass of water:

items.text: Stop pouring when the glass is full

feedback.correct: Glass first, then pour, then stop. Order matters.
feedback.incorrect: Can you pour into a glass you haven't picked up yet?

content.question: What happens if step 3 (stop pouring) happens BEFORE step 2 (pour water)?

options.text: You stop before you ever start, so no water gets poured
The computer figures out what you meant and pours the water anyway
You get double the water
The glass breaks

content.explanation: Computers do not rearrange steps to make them make sense. They execute the exact order given.

feedback.correct: Right. Stopping before starting means nothing happens.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: the computer executes step by step, strictly in order.

content.question:
Here are instructions for turning on a lamp:
1. Flip the switch.
2. Plug the lamp into the wall.

Why did the lamp not turn on when step 1 happened?

options.text: The lamp had no electricity yet when the switch was flipped
The lamp is broken
The switch was flipped too fast
The lightbulb needs replacement

content.explanation: Step order creates preconditions. Step 2 created the precondition that step 1 required.

feedback.correct: Exactly. Flipping the switch before plugging it in does nothing. Preconditions must be met in order.
feedback.incorrect: Look at what each step makes possible: does flipping a switch work without power?

content.prompt: Arrange all four steps into the correct order to make a sandwich:

items.text: Spread peanut butter on the first slice
Place the second slice on top
Place two slices of bread on the plate
Spread jelly on top of the peanut butter

feedback.correct: Bread first, peanut butter, jelly, close. Every precondition was met before the next step.
feedback.incorrect: Trace through step by step: what must exist before you can spread on it?

content.question: What is the single most important rule about computer instructions?

options.text: Computers execute instructions literally, in the exact sequence given, without guessing what you meant
Computers understand English if you type clearly
Computers will fix mistakes if the instructions run fast enough
Step order doesn't matter as long as all steps are included

content.explanation: This is the foundational mental model of all programming: literal sequential execution.

feedback.correct: That is the core rule. Computers execute literally, in sequence, without guessing.
feedback.incorrect: Think about the sandwich: did the computer guess what you meant?

content.question:
A developer writes code that creates a button, then adds it to the page, then styles it blue.
What does the browser do?

options.text: It executes each step in order: creates the button, places it, then applies the blue style
It styles the button first because blue is pretty
It skips creating the button and just draws blue
It does all three at the exact same millisecond with no sequence

content.explanation: The browser is just like the literal assistant: it executes instructions in the exact sequence written.

feedback.correct: Right. Code is just precise instructions executed in order. The same rule applies everywhere.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: the computer has no preferences. It executes the steps in the sequence written.

content.question: If you try to style a button BEFORE creating it in code, what will happen?

options.text: The computer fails because you cannot style something that doesn't exist yet
The computer waits patiently until the button is created later
The computer automatically creates the button for you
Nothing happens, but the style applies anyway

content.explanation: Just like putting cheese on bread before getting the bread: attempting to use an object before creating it causes an error.

feedback.correct: Exactly. You cannot style what does not exist yet. Preconditions must be created first.
feedback.incorrect: Can you put cheese on bread that isn't on the plate yet?

content.title: Forge Takeaway
takeaways: Computers execute instructions literally, step by step.
Order matters: a step cannot use something a previous step hasn't created yet.
When code fails, the computer didn't get confused—the instructions were flawed or in the wrong order.

feedback.correct: You have mastered the foundational mental model of computer execution.
